newsitem.title: USA: U.S. manufacturers urge liability bill passage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. manufacturers urge liability bill passage.

text.p: The National Association of Manufacturers Tuesday launched another effort to win passage of a bill limiting product liability damages, saying the suits were hurting the competitiveness of American businesses.

"We have clearly reached a crisis point," NAM President Jerry Jasinowski said at a news conference. "Product liability costs in the U.S. are 15 times greater than Japan's and 20 times greater than Europe's."

The bill the NAM and other business groups back would limit punitive damages in product liability cases to twice the amount of compensatory damages, or $250,000, whichever is greater. Supporters say the bill is needed to curb excessive damage awards and to discourage frivolous lawsuits.

Congress passed a similar bill last year, but President Bill Clinton vetoed it, and the veto was sustained. Clinton said the bill went too far in limiting damages for injury victims, but the bill's supporters said he was influenced by large campaign contributions from trial lawyers who opposed the limits.
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi has made the bill one of his top 10 legislative priorities.

Freshman Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Alabama, also urged passage of the bill. "This bill will help put limits on lawsuits, keep innocent third parties from being drawn into litigation and reduced unjustified litigation expenses," Sessions said.
Jasinowski said nine out of 10 businesses have or can expect to be involved in a product liability case. He said the suits were especially costly to small businesses.
NAM members were asked at a breakfast meeting at the U.S. Capitol to urge their senators and representatives and Clinton to support the bill.
